metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Critical data center equipment now takes years rather than months to arrive, and delivery schedules gate construction as hard as permits do.

The constraint has moved from money to manufacturing. Capital expenditure is tracked as a sibling metric, and capital can be committed far faster than transformers, switchgear, generators, and cooling plant can be built. Those are fabricated, engineered items with limited production lines, not commodities a buyer can source on demand. When order-to-delivery stretches from months to years, a funded project still waits.

For AI this matters because compute is downstream of buildings and power. A cluster of accelerators does nothing until the shell exists, the utility feed is stepped down through transformers and switchgear, and the heat is removed by cooling plant. Accelerators appear in the same lead-time list as the electrical gear, which means compute procurement and electrical procurement share one schedule. The pace of AI scaling is therefore set partly by supply chains that have nothing to do with chips.

What the data does not carry is the numbers. It gives the direction of travel and the equipment categories, not current lead times by item, not regional differences, not vendor names, not prices, and not whether the trend is still worsening or has flattened. It also does not say how much of a typical construction schedule the equipment delay accounts for relative to permitting. Those gaps are where the actual forecasting would happen.
